claims.text: A thin Nb-doped surface coating on CoCrFeNi promotes in-situ formation of a stable oxide scale during sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
The in-situ oxide scale is lubricious.
The Nb-doped coating reduces friction relative to untreated CoCrFeNi.
The Nb-doped coating reduces wear relative to untreated CoCrFeNi.
Physical vapor deposition is a possible method for applying the thin Nb-doped surface treatment.
The treatment produces a robust Nb-containing oxide scale at the sliding interface.
Nb incorporation alters oxidation kinetics under sliding conditions.
Altered oxidation kinetics generate a self-adaptive, lubricious oxide layer.
At lower temperatures, the coating itself can reduce friction.
At elevated temperatures, the in-situ oxide scale provides a low-shear interface.
At elevated temperatures, the in-situ oxide scale improves wear resistance.
The treated alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than untreated CoCrFeNi throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
The treated alloy will have a lower wear rate than untreated CoCrFeNi throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
Untreated CoCrFeNi demonstrates acceptable tribological performance at room temperature.
Untreated CoCrFeNi suffers elevated friction at high temperatures.
Untreated CoCrFeNi suffers elevated wear at high temperatures.
The proposed applicability range is ambient air, moderate normal loads, and approximately 25–800 °C.

contradictions.description: The mechanism allows low-temperature friction reduction to arise from the coating itself, but the falsification rule treats failure to observe the Nb-containing oxide scale across the entire temperature range as falsifying the hypothesis. Thus, absence of oxide at low temperature could trigger falsification even though the stated low-temperature mechanism does not require that oxide.
